TITLE: AI Benchmarks Explained: MMLU, GPQA, SWE-bench, Humanity's Last Exam and More
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: What do AI benchmark scores like MMLU, GPQA Diamond, SWE-bench Verified, AIME, Humanity's Last Exam, ARC-AGI and LMArena actually measure? A plain-English guide to the most cited LLM benchmarks, how to read them, and why scores can mislead.
KEY: AI benchmarks are standardised tests used to compare AI models. Each measures a specific skill: MMLU tests broad knowledge, GPQA Diamond tests expert-level science, AIME tests competition maths, SWE-bench Verified tests fixing real software bugs, Humanity's Last Exam tests frontier knowledge, ARC-AGI tests novel reasoning, and LMArena ranks models by human votes. Benchmarks are useful signals, but scores can be inflated by training-data contamination and quickly "saturate", so always test models on your own tasks.
content:
Short answer

AI benchmarks are standardised tests used to compare AI models. Each measures a specific skill: MMLU tests broad knowledge, GPQA Diamond tests expert-level science, AIME tests competition maths, SWE-bench Verified tests fixing real software bugs, Humanity's Last Exam tests frontier knowledge, ARC-AGI tests novel reasoning, and LMArena ranks models by human votes. Benchmarks are useful signals, but scores can be inflated by training-data contamination and quickly "saturate", so always test models on your own tasks.

Why benchmarks matter

When a new model launches, its announcement is full of scores. Benchmarks give a common yardstick to compare large language models from different labs, track progress over time and spot strengths and weaknesses. For a live comparison of models, see our LLM benchmarks page.

The most cited AI benchmarks

Knowledge: MMLU and MMLU-Pro

MMLU (2020) contains about 16,000 multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, from law to medicine. Top models now score around 90%, so it no longer separates them well. MMLU-Pro adds harder questions with ten answer options.

Expert science: GPQA Diamond

GPQA questions were written by PhD experts and designed so that skilled non-experts with web access still get most wrong. The Diamond subset of 198 questions is the most quoted version and a common test of reasoning models.

Maths: AIME and beyond

AIME problems require multi-step reasoning with exact answers, making them hard to guess. Scores jumped dramatically once labs trained models with reinforcement learning to reason step by step; see What is reinforcement learning?. Harder maths benchmarks such as FrontierMath now test research-level problems.

Coding: SWE-bench Verified and HumanEval

HumanEval (2021) checks whether generated functions pass unit tests; most frontier models now ace it. SWE-bench gives a model a real repository and a real bug report and checks whether its fix passes the project's tests. The Verified subset of 500 human-checked tasks, released in 2024, is the main benchmark for coding agents and vibe coding tools.

Frontier knowledge: Humanity's Last Exam

Released in January 2025 by the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI, HLE gathered very difficult questions from experts worldwide, keeping only those that leading models failed at the time. It was designed to stay challenging after older benchmarks saturated.

Novel reasoning: ARC-AGI

Created by François Chollet, ARC-AGI shows a few example grid transformations and asks the model to infer the rule for a new grid. The puzzles are easy for most people but hard for AI because they cannot be memorised. ARC-AGI-2, launched in 2025, raised the difficulty further. See What is AGI? for why this matters.

Human preference: LMArena

LMArena shows users two anonymous answers to the same prompt and asks which is better. Thousands of votes produce a leaderboard. It captures helpfulness and style but can reward length and formatting over correctness.

How to read benchmark scores

  • Check the exact setting: pass@1 (one attempt) is stricter than pass@k or "with majority voting".
  • Tools allowed? Scores with code execution or web search are not comparable with scores without them.
  • Reasoning effort: reasoning models often report results at their highest thinking budget, which is slower and costlier.
  • Who ran it? Independent evaluations are more trustworthy than self-reported numbers.
  • Small differences: a gap of one or two points is often within noise.

Why benchmarks can mislead

  • Contamination: test questions leak into training data from the web, so a model may have memorised answers.
  • Saturation: once top models score 90%+, the benchmark stops distinguishing them.
  • Goodhart's law: when a score becomes a target, labs optimise for it, sometimes at the expense of real usefulness.
  • Narrow coverage: no benchmark captures everything you care about, such as writing quality, honesty, safety or speed.
  • Cost and latency ignored: a model that scores slightly higher may be far more expensive to run. See how much energy AI uses.

How to evaluate models for your own use

1. Collect 20 to 100 real examples of your task with good reference answers. 2. Run several candidate models with the same prompt and settings. 3. Score answers for correctness, format and usefulness, by hand or with a strong model as judge, spot-checked by a person. 4. Weigh quality against cost, speed and privacy, including small language models you can run locally.

Hardware benchmarks are different

AI hardware is measured with benchmarks such as MLPerf (training and inference speed on standard models), tokens per second and cost per million tokens. These depend on GPU memory bandwidth, precision and software. See GPU memory bandwidth, the LLM inference simulator and our GPU cloud price tracker.

Frequently asked questions

Which benchmark is most important?

It depends on your use case: SWE-bench for coding, GPQA and HLE for expert knowledge, AIME for maths, MMMU for images, and LMArena for general chat preference.

Why do new benchmarks keep appearing?

Models improve so quickly that older tests saturate within a year or two, so researchers create harder ones to keep measuring progress.

Can companies cheat on benchmarks?

Deliberate cheating is rare, but contamination, selective reporting and tuning for specific benchmarks happen. Independent and held-out evaluations help.

Do higher benchmark scores mean a model is smarter?

They mean it performs better on those tests. Real-world usefulness also depends on reliability, speed, cost, safety and fit for your task.

Sources and further reading

  • Hendrycks et al., Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU, 2020)
  • Rein et al., GPQA: A Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark (2023)
  • Jimenez et al., SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues? (2023)
  • Phan et al., Humanity's Last Exam (2025)
  • Chollet, On the Measure of Intelligence (ARC, 2019)
  • MLCommons MLPerf benchmarks

TITLE: How Much Energy Does AI Use? Data Centers, ChatGPT Prompts and GPUs Explained
LABEL: EXPLAINER
IMG: How Much Energy Does AI Use?
EXCERPT: How much electricity does AI really use? Data center energy demand, the energy of a single AI prompt, the cost of training large models, why GPUs draw so much power, water use, and what is being done to make AI more efficient.
KEY: AI's energy use is growing fast but is often misunderstood. The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates data centers used about 415 TWh of electricity in 2024 (around 1.5% of global electricity) and projects this will more than double to about 945 TWh by 2030, with AI the main driver. A single chatbot text prompt is small: Google measured the median Gemini text prompt at about 0.24 watt-hours, roughly like running a TV for nine seconds. The big totals come from billions of prompts, longer reasoning and video generation, and from training ever-larger models on tens of thousands of GPUs.
content:
Short answer

AI's energy use is growing fast but is often misunderstood. The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates data centers used about 415 TWh of electricity in 2024 (around 1.5% of global electricity) and projects this will more than double to about 945 TWh by 2030, with AI the main driver. A single chatbot text prompt is small: Google measured the median Gemini text prompt at about 0.24 watt-hours, roughly like running a TV for nine seconds. The big totals come from billions of prompts, longer reasoning and video generation, and from training ever-larger models on tens of thousands of GPUs.

The big picture: data centers

AI data centers are buildings full of GPU servers, networking, storage and cooling. According to the IEA's 2025 *Energy and AI* report:

  • Data centers used roughly 415 TWh in 2024, about 1.5% of the world's electricity.
  • Demand is projected to reach about 945 TWh by 2030, slightly more than Japan uses today.
  • AI-focused, accelerated servers are the fastest-growing part of that demand.
  • The United States and China account for most of the growth.

Data centers are still a modest share of total global electricity, but they are concentrated: in some regions they already use a large share of local supply, which strains grids and drives new power plant and transmission projects.

How much energy does one AI prompt use?

Google's measurement included the AI chips, host servers, idle capacity and data center overhead, and also reported about 0.26 ml of water per median prompt. Estimates vary a lot by model size, answer length and hardware, so treat single numbers as rough guides.

Two trends push per-prompt energy in opposite directions:

  • Efficiency gains: newer GPUs, low-precision formats like FP8 and FP4, better software and mixture-of-experts models make each token cheaper. Google reported large year-on-year reductions in energy per prompt.
  • Heavier use: reasoning models generate thousands of hidden tokens, AI agents run many steps, and video generation is far more compute-intensive than text.

How much energy does training use?

Training a frontier model runs thousands of GPUs non-stop for weeks or months. A widely cited 2021 study estimated that training GPT-3 used about 1,287 MWh, roughly what 120 average US homes use in a year. Today's largest models are trained with far more compute on clusters of tens of thousands of GPUs, so their training runs use much more, though developers rarely publish exact figures. See AI training vs inference and LLM training cost for how the compute adds up.

Over a popular model's lifetime, inference (answering users) usually uses more total energy than training, because it runs billions of times.

Why AI hardware draws so much power

Modern AI chips pack tens of billions of transistors that switch billions of times per second, and moving data between memory and compute costs energy too. That is why memory bandwidth and stacked HBM close to the chip matter for efficiency. Dense racks like the GB200 NVL72 need liquid cooling because air cannot remove that much heat.

Water use

Data centers use water mainly for cooling, either directly (evaporative cooling) or indirectly through the power plants that supply electricity. Usage depends heavily on climate and cooling design. Closed-loop liquid cooling and siting in cooler climates reduce water consumption, and many operators report water use per unit of compute.

How AI is getting more efficient

  • Better chips: each GPU generation delivers far more AI performance per watt. See Hopper vs Blackwell.
  • Lower precision: NVFP4 and FP8 do more work per joule than FP16.
  • Smarter models: small language models, distillation and MoE give similar quality with less compute.
  • Software: techniques like FlashAttention, batching and KV cache optimisation squeeze more tokens from each GPU.
  • Specialised chips: AI accelerators such as TPUs and inference ASICs can be more efficient for specific workloads.
  • On-device AI: running small models on phones and AI PCs avoids data center trips for simple tasks.
  • Clean power: tech companies are signing large deals for solar, wind, nuclear and geothermal power.

What you can do

  • Use smaller or faster models for simple tasks, and reasoning modes only when needed.
  • Avoid regenerating answers or images many times without reason.
  • Run small models locally when it makes sense; see how to run an LLM locally.

Frequently asked questions

Does one ChatGPT question use a bottle of water?

No. That claim came from early, broad estimates. Google's 2025 measurement put a median Gemini text prompt at about 0.26 ml of water, a few drops. Totals become significant at the scale of billions of prompts.

Is AI worse for energy than Bitcoin mining?

They are different kinds of demand. Estimates for Bitcoin are in a similar range to today's AI share of data center use, but AI demand is growing faster and also delivers useful services. Both depend heavily on how clean the electricity is.

Will AI cause power shortages?

In specific regions with many new data centers, grid capacity is a real constraint, and utilities are investing heavily. Globally, the IEA expects data centers to remain a relatively small share of electricity growth compared with industry, air conditioning and electric vehicles.

How much power does a home AI PC use?

A desktop with a high-end GPU can draw 500 to 800 W under full AI load, but local AI usually runs in short bursts. Smaller models on laptops and Macs use far less.

Sources and further reading

  • International Energy Agency, Energy and AI: Energy demand from AI (2025)
  • Google Cloud, Measuring the environmental impact of AI inference (August 2025)
  • Patterson et al., Carbon Emissions and Large Neural Network Training (2021)
  • Data Center Dynamics, IEA: data center energy consumption set to double by 2030 to 945 TWh (2025)

TITLE: How Neural Networks Learn: Gradient Descent and Backpropagation Explained Simply
LABEL: EXPLAINER
EXCERPT: Gradient descent and backpropagation are how every neural network, from image classifiers to ChatGPT, learns. A plain-English guide to loss, gradients, learning rate, SGD and Adam, the chain rule behind backprop, and why GPUs and tensor cores make it fast.
KEY: Neural networks learn with two ideas working together. Backpropagation works out how much each of the model's millions or billions of weights contributed to an error. Gradient descent then nudges every weight a small step in the direction that reduces that error. Repeated over billions of examples, these tiny adjustments turn random numbers into a model that can recognise images or write text. Almost all of the work is matrix multiplication, which is exactly what GPUs and tensor cores are built for.
content:
Short answer

Neural networks learn with two ideas working together. Backpropagation works out how much each of the model's millions or billions of weights contributed to an error. Gradient descent then nudges every weight a small step in the direction that reduces that error. Repeated over billions of examples, these tiny adjustments turn random numbers into a model that can recognise images or write text. Almost all of the work is matrix multiplication, which is exactly what GPUs and tensor cores are built for.

Step 1: Measure the error with a loss function

A neural network makes a prediction, for example "80% cat". We compare it with the right answer using a loss function, a single number that is large when the model is wrong and small when it is right. Common choices are cross-entropy for classification and next-token prediction, and mean squared error for predicting numbers.

Training means finding the weights that make the average loss as small as possible.

Step 2: Gradient descent, walking downhill

Imagine standing on a foggy mountain and wanting to reach the valley. You cannot see far, but you can feel the slope under your feet. The sensible strategy: take a step downhill, feel the slope again, repeat.

That is gradient descent:

  • The loss landscape is the mountain: every possible setting of the weights has a height (the loss).
  • The gradient is the slope: it tells you which direction increases the loss fastest, so you step the opposite way.
  • The learning rate is your step size.

The update rule for each weight is simply:

new_weight = old_weight - learning_rate × gradient

Choosing the learning rate

  • Too large: you overshoot the valley and the loss jumps around or explodes.
  • Too small: training takes forever or gets stuck.
  • In practice: most training uses a schedule, warming up the learning rate at the start and lowering it gradually later.

Step 3: Backpropagation, finding every gradient

A large model has billions of weights. Backpropagation computes the gradient for all of them efficiently in one backward sweep:

1. Forward pass: feed the input through the network, layer by layer, to get a prediction and the loss. 2. Backward pass: starting from the loss, apply the chain rule from calculus layer by layer in reverse, calculating how much each weight affected the final error. 3. Update: use gradient descent to adjust every weight.

The chain rule is the key idea: if A affects B and B affects C, then the effect of A on C is the effect of A on B multiplied by the effect of B on C. Backprop applies this through every layer. The method was popularised for neural networks by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams in 1986, and modern frameworks such as PyTorch do it automatically ("autograd").

Variants of gradient descent

Adam keeps two extra numbers per weight (running averages of gradients and squared gradients). That is one reason training needs far more memory than running a model: roughly 16 bytes per parameter in mixed precision. See AI training vs inference and mixed precision training.

Common problems and fixes

  • Vanishing gradients: gradients shrink to almost zero in deep networks, so early layers stop learning. Fixed by ReLU-style activations, residual connections and normalisation layers.
  • Exploding gradients: gradients grow huge and destabilise training. Fixed with gradient clipping and careful initialisation.
  • Overfitting: the model memorises training data. Countered with more data, regularisation, dropout and early stopping.
  • Local minima and saddle points: in very high-dimensional networks these are less of a problem than once feared; noise from mini-batches helps escape flat regions.
  • Number precision: very small gradients can underflow in FP16, which is why BF16 and loss scaling are used. See FP16 vs BF16 vs FP8.

Why GPUs make this fast

Both the forward and backward passes are dominated by multiplying large matrices: activations times weights, and gradients times activations. The backward pass costs about twice as much as the forward pass, giving the rule of thumb that training costs about 6 FLOPs per parameter per token. GPUs with thousands of cores and tensor cores run these matrix operations massively in parallel; see how a GPU works and What is a GPU?. Large models split the work across many GPUs in a GPU cluster, averaging gradients between them after each step.

A tiny example in Python

Fitting y = 3x with one weight:

w = 0.0
lr = 0.1
data = [(1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9)]
for step in range(50):
    grad = sum(2 * (w * x - y) * x for x, y in data) / len(data)
    w -= lr * grad
print(round(w, 3))  # approaches 3.0

Real networks do the same thing with billions of weights at once.

Frequently asked questions

Is backpropagation the same as gradient descent?

No. Backpropagation calculates the gradients; gradient descent uses them to update the weights. Training needs both.

Does the brain use backpropagation?

Probably not in the same way. Neuroscientists are still debating how the brain learns, and backprop is considered biologically unlikely in its exact form.

Do LLMs learn during a conversation?

No. Gradient descent only happens during training or fine-tuning. During a chat the weights are fixed; the model only uses what is in its context window.

Why is the learning rate so important?

It controls the size of every update. A good learning rate and schedule often matter more than other training settings.

Sources and further reading

  • Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, Learning representations by back-propagating errors (Nature, 1986)
  • Kingma and Ba, Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization (2014)
  • Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning (MIT Press, 2016)
  • PyTorch, A gentle introduction to torch.autograd

TITLE: LLM Temperature, Top-k and Top-p Explained: Best Settings for ChatGPT and Local Models
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: Temperature, top-k, top-p and min-p control how random or predictable an AI model's answers are. What each setting does, how they work under the hood, recommended values for coding, writing and chat, and common mistakes.
KEY: Temperature controls how random a language model's output is. At each step the model scores every possible next token; a low temperature (0 to 0.3) makes it almost always pick the most likely token, giving focused, repeatable answers, while a high temperature (0.8 to 1.2) spreads the choice more widely for more varied, creative text. Top-k and top-p limit which tokens are allowed at all. For most uses, adjust temperature or top-p, not both.
content:
Short answer

Temperature controls how random a language model's output is. At each step the model scores every possible next token; a low temperature (0 to 0.3) makes it almost always pick the most likely token, giving focused, repeatable answers, while a high temperature (0.8 to 1.2) spreads the choice more widely for more varied, creative text. Top-k and top-p limit which tokens are allowed at all. For most uses, adjust temperature or top-p, not both.

How a model chooses the next word

A large language model does not output a word directly. At each step it produces a score (a "logit") for every token in its vocabulary, often 100,000 or more. These scores are turned into probabilities with the softmax function. Then one token is sampled from those probabilities, appended to the text, and the process repeats.

Sampling settings decide how that choice is made. You can see this live in our LLM sampling simulator.

Temperature

Before softmax, every score is divided by the temperature:

probability(token) ∝ exp(score / temperature)
  • Temperature below 1: differences between scores grow, so the top token dominates.
  • Temperature = 1: the model's original probabilities.
  • Temperature above 1: probabilities even out, so unlikely tokens get chosen more often.
  • Temperature = 0: in practice means "always pick the most likely token" (greedy decoding).

Example: suppose the next word after "The GPU has 80 GB of" has these probabilities at temperature 1: "memory" 70%, "VRAM" 20%, "HBM3" 8%, "cheese" 2%. At temperature 0.3, "memory" rises to about 98%. At temperature 1.5, "cheese" more than doubles to about 5%, which is how high temperatures produce odd or incoherent text.

Top-k sampling

Top-k keeps only the k most likely tokens and samples among them. With top-k = 40, the model can never pick a token outside the top 40. It prevents rare nonsense, but a fixed k can be too strict when many words fit, or too loose when only one does.

Top-p (nucleus) sampling

Top-p keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p. With top-p = 0.9, the model samples only from tokens that together make up 90% of the probability. When the model is confident, that might be one or two tokens; when many continuations are plausible, it might be hundreds. This adaptivity made top-p a popular default.

Min-p sampling

Min-p keeps tokens whose probability is at least a fraction of the top token's probability (for example 5% of it). It is popular in local LLM tools because it stays coherent even at higher temperatures.

Other settings you may see

  • Frequency and presence penalties: reduce repetition by penalising tokens that already appeared.
  • Repetition penalty: the local-model equivalent, common in llama.cpp and Ollama.
  • Max tokens: caps the length of the response.
  • Seed: fixes the random choices so results can be reproduced.
  • Stop sequences: strings that end generation.

Recommended settings

Always start from the model provider's recommended defaults; some models are tuned for specific values. Many reasoning models fix or ignore temperature because their training assumes particular settings; see What is a reasoning model?.

Common mistakes

  • Lowering temperature to stop hallucinations: low temperature makes answers more consistent, not more correct. A model can confidently repeat the same wrong fact at temperature 0. Use RAG, sources and verification instead; see AI hallucinations.
  • Changing temperature and top-p at the same time: their effects overlap and become hard to reason about.
  • Expecting temperature 0 to be perfectly deterministic: small numerical differences on GPUs and batching can still change outputs.
  • Using high temperature for code: it introduces typos and logic errors.

Where to change these settings

  • ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini apps: usually fixed; you control style through your prompt.
  • APIs and playgrounds: set temperature, top_p and sometimes top_k in each request.
  • Local tools: Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp expose temperature, top-k, top-p, min-p and repetition penalty. See how to run an LLM locally.

Does sampling affect speed or hardware?

Very little. Sampling is a tiny calculation compared with running the model itself, whose speed depends mainly on memory bandwidth and model size. Generating several alternative answers, however, multiplies the compute.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best temperature for ChatGPT-style chat?

Around 0.7 is a common balance between natural and reliable. Use lower values for factual or technical work.

Is temperature 0 always best for accuracy?

It is best for consistency. For some reasoning tasks, generating several answers at a moderate temperature and picking the most common one can be more accurate.

What is the difference between top-k and top-p?

Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens; top-p keeps a variable number based on cumulative probability. Top-p adapts better to how confident the model is.

Why is it called temperature?

The term comes from statistical physics, where higher temperature means particles move more randomly, just as higher sampling temperature makes token choices more random.

Sources and further reading

  • Holtzman et al., The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration (nucleus sampling, 2019)
  • Fan et al., Hierarchical Neural Story Generation (top-k sampling, 2018)
  • Nguyen et al., Turning Up the Heat: Min-p Sampling for Creative and Coherent LLM Outputs (2024)
  • OpenAI, API reference: chat completions

TITLE: What Is an AI Accelerator? GPUs, TPUs, NPUs and AI Chips Explained
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: An AI accelerator is a chip designed to run artificial intelligence workloads faster and more efficiently than a general-purpose CPU. The main types (GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, custom ASICs, wafer-scale chips and FPGAs), how they work, who makes them and how to compare them.
KEY: An AI accelerator is a processor specialised for the maths of neural networks, mainly huge matrix multiplications, so it can train and run AI models far faster and more efficiently than a general-purpose CPU. The main types are GPUs (NVIDIA, AMD), TPUs (Google), NPUs in phones and laptops, custom ASICs built by cloud companies (such as AWS Trainium), and novel designs like Cerebras' wafer-scale chip and Groq's LPU. NVIDIA GPUs dominate today, but competition is growing fast.
content:
Short answer

An AI accelerator is a processor specialised for the maths of neural networks, mainly huge matrix multiplications, so it can train and run AI models far faster and more efficiently than a general-purpose CPU. The main types are GPUs (NVIDIA, AMD), TPUs (Google), NPUs in phones and laptops, custom ASICs built by cloud companies (such as AWS Trainium), and novel designs like Cerebras' wafer-scale chip and Groq's LPU. NVIDIA GPUs dominate today, but competition is growing fast.

Why AI needs special chips

A neural network is mostly multiplying large grids of numbers, billions or trillions of times. CPUs are built to run varied, branching code one step after another on a few powerful cores. AI work is the opposite: the same simple operation repeated in parallel on enormous amounts of data. Accelerators devote most of their silicon to parallel arithmetic units and fast memory, and support low-precision number formats (FP8, FP4, INT8) that pack more operations into each clock cycle and each watt. See GPU vs CPU for AI.

Types of AI accelerators

GPUs

GPUs began as graphics chips and became the default AI accelerator after CUDA made them programmable for general computing. Modern NVIDIA GPUs contain tensor cores, dedicated matrix units that deliver most of their AI performance. Their biggest advantage is software: CUDA, cuDNN, TensorRT and support in every major framework. See What is a GPU? and AMD vs NVIDIA for AI.

TPUs

Google's Tensor Processing Units use large systolic arrays, grids of multiply-accumulate units through which data flows rhythmically, minimising memory traffic. Google trains its Gemini models on TPUs and rents them to cloud customers. See TPU vs GPU, Google Ironwood and Google TPU 8tx and 8i Max.

NPUs

Neural processing units are small, power-efficient accelerators built into phone and laptop processors for on-device features. See NPU vs GPU vs TPU, What is an AI PC? and What is edge AI?.

Custom ASICs

Application-specific integrated circuits are designed for one purpose. Cloud giants build their own to reduce dependence on NVIDIA and cut costs: Amazon's Trainium and Inferentia, Microsoft's Maia, Meta's MTIA and others. Chip designers such as Broadcom help several companies build custom AI chips.

Wafer-scale and dataflow chips

Cerebras builds a single chip the size of a whole silicon wafer with massive on-chip SRAM, avoiding slow off-chip memory for many workloads; see Cerebras WSE-3. Groq's LPU uses a deterministic design focused on fast inference; see Groq LPU vs GPU.

What makes an accelerator fast

  • Compute (TFLOPS/TOPS): how many operations per second, which depends heavily on precision. See TOPS vs TFLOPS.
  • Memory capacity: how big a model fits. Data center chips use stacked HBM.
  • Memory bandwidth: how fast weights and data reach the compute units, often the real bottleneck for chatbots. See GPU memory bandwidth and the roofline model simulator.
  • Interconnect: how fast chips talk to each other in a cluster, such as NVIDIA NVLink and NVSwitch.
  • Precision support: FP8 and FP4 formats such as NVFP4 double or quadruple throughput.
  • Software: compilers, libraries and framework support often matter more than raw specs.
  • Power efficiency: performance per watt drives data center costs. See how much energy AI uses.

Training vs inference accelerators

Training needs high compute, large memory and fast interconnects across thousands of chips. Inference needs low latency, high memory bandwidth and low cost per token. Some chips target both (NVIDIA GPUs, TPUs), while others focus on inference (Inferentia, Groq, many startups). See AI training vs inference.

How to compare AI accelerators

1. Check dense performance at the precision you will use (sparse figures are often doubled). 2. Compare memory capacity and bandwidth against your model size. 3. Consider software support for your frameworks and models. 4. Look at availability and price: many accelerators are only available in specific clouds. Our GPU cloud price tracker compares GPU rental prices daily. 5. Read the spec sheet carefully; see how to read a GPU spec sheet.

Frequently asked questions

Is a GPU an AI accelerator?

Yes. GPUs are general-purpose parallel processors, but modern data center GPUs are designed primarily as AI accelerators and are the most widely used type.

Why does NVIDIA dominate AI chips?

A combination of strong hardware, early investment in AI, and above all the CUDA software ecosystem that most AI code is built on, plus complete systems including networking.

Can I buy a TPU?

Not as a standalone data center chip for your own servers in the usual way; Google offers TPUs through Google Cloud. Small Edge TPU devices exist for hobby and embedded projects.

What is the fastest AI chip?

It depends on the workload. For large-scale training, NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs and Google's latest TPUs lead; for single-user token speed, specialised chips like Cerebras and Groq post very high numbers. See B200 vs H100 and MI355X vs B200.

Sources and further reading

  • Jouppi et al., In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit (2017)
  • NVIDIA, Blackwell architecture
  • AWS, Trainium
  • Cerebras, Wafer-Scale Engine

TITLE: What Is Computer Vision? How AI Sees and Understands Images
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: Computer vision is the field of AI that teaches computers to understand images and video. Core tasks like classification, object detection and segmentation, how CNNs and vision transformers work, real-world uses, and the hardware behind it.
KEY: Computer vision is the branch of artificial intelligence that enables computers to interpret and understand images and video: recognising objects, reading text, tracking movement and measuring the world. It powers phone face unlock, self-driving cars, medical image analysis, factory inspection and photo search. Modern computer vision relies on deep learning, first convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and now increasingly vision transformers, trained on millions of labelled images and run on GPUs and edge AI chips.
content:
Short answer

Computer vision is the branch of artificial intelligence that enables computers to interpret and understand images and video: recognising objects, reading text, tracking movement and measuring the world. It powers phone face unlock, self-driving cars, medical image analysis, factory inspection and photo search. Modern computer vision relies on deep learning, first convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and now increasingly vision transformers, trained on millions of labelled images and run on GPUs and edge AI chips.

What computers "see"

To a computer, an image is just a grid of numbers: each pixel has values for red, green and blue. A 12-megapixel photo is 36 million numbers. Computer vision is about turning those numbers into meaning: "this is a cat", "there is a pedestrian 20 metres ahead", "this weld is cracked".

Core computer vision tasks

How computer vision works

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs)

A CNN slides small filters across an image to detect simple patterns such as edges and corners in early layers, then combines them into textures, parts (eyes, wheels) and whole objects in deeper layers. The breakthrough came in 2012 when AlexNet, a CNN trained on GPUs, won the ImageNet challenge by a wide margin. ResNet (2015) made very deep networks trainable and became a standard backbone.

Vision transformers (ViT)

In 2020, researchers showed that the transformer architecture from language AI works for images too: split the image into patches, treat each patch like a token and use attention to relate them. Vision transformers scale very well with data and are the basis of many modern vision and multimodal models.

Foundation models for vision

Instead of training a new model for every task, large pre-trained models can be reused:

  • CLIP learns to match images with text, enabling search like "photos of red cars at night".
  • Segment Anything (SAM) from Meta can cut out almost any object from a click or prompt.
  • YOLO models provide fast real-time object detection on modest hardware.
  • Vision language models answer questions about images in plain language.

The training pipeline

1. Collect and label images (boxes, masks or captions). 2. Train or fine-tune a model on that data. 3. Evaluate on images it has never seen. 4. Deploy in the cloud or on edge devices, often with quantization to make it smaller and faster.

Real-world uses

  • Smartphones: face unlock, portrait mode, photo search, live translation of signs.
  • Automotive: driver assistance, lane keeping, self-driving perception.
  • Healthcare: helping radiologists spot findings in X-rays, CT scans and pathology slides.
  • Manufacturing: detecting defects on production lines.
  • Retail: checkout-free stores, shelf monitoring, visual product search.
  • Agriculture: crop health monitoring from drones and satellites.
  • Security: intrusion detection and access control, which raises important privacy questions.
  • Documents: OCR for invoices, IDs and forms.
  • Robotics: grasping objects and navigating spaces.

Challenges

  • Data and labelling: good training data is expensive to collect and annotate.
  • Edge cases: rare situations (unusual weather, odd objects) cause errors, which is critical for self-driving.
  • Bias: models can perform worse for groups under-represented in training data.
  • Adversarial examples: small, deliberate changes to images can fool models.
  • Privacy: facial recognition and surveillance are tightly regulated in many places, including under the EU AI Act.

Hardware for computer vision

  • Training uses GPUs with plenty of VRAM; vision models are generally smaller than LLMs, so a single consumer GPU can train or fine-tune many of them.
  • Real-time inference on cameras, robots and cars uses edge AI hardware such as NVIDIA Jetson modules and NPUs in phones and AI PCs.
  • Large-scale video analytics in the cloud uses data center GPUs, which also include hardware video decoders.

Tensor cores speed up the convolutions and matrix multiplications that dominate vision workloads.

Frequently asked questions

Is computer vision the same as image processing?

No. Image processing changes images (sharpening, resizing, filtering). Computer vision extracts meaning from them. Vision systems often use image processing as a first step.

What programming language is used for computer vision?

Python is the most common, with libraries such as OpenCV, PyTorch, torchvision and Ultralytics YOLO.

How accurate is computer vision?

On standard benchmarks, top models match or exceed human accuracy for many recognition tasks, but real-world accuracy depends on lighting, camera quality and how closely conditions match the training data.

Is computer vision part of generative AI?

Traditional computer vision analyses images; generative AI creates them. The fields overlap heavily and share architectures. See What is generative AI?.

Sources and further reading

  • Krizhevsky et al., ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (2012)
  • He et al., Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition (2015)
  • Dosovitskiy et al., An Image is Worth 16x16 Words (2020)
  • Kirillov et al., Segment Anything (2023)

TITLE: What Is Edge AI? Running AI on Devices Instead of the Cloud
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: Edge AI runs artificial intelligence directly on devices such as phones, cameras, cars, robots and PCs instead of in distant data centers. How edge AI works, its benefits for speed and privacy, the NPUs and modules that power it, examples and limits.
KEY: Edge AI means running AI models directly on a local device, such as a smartphone, laptop, security camera, car, drone, robot or factory sensor, instead of sending data to a cloud data center. Processing data where it is created gives faster responses, better privacy, lower bandwidth costs and offline operation. Edge AI runs on efficient chips like the NPUs in phones and AI PCs, NVIDIA Jetson modules and small GPUs, usually with compact, quantized models.
content:
Short answer

Edge AI means running AI models directly on a local device, such as a smartphone, laptop, security camera, car, drone, robot or factory sensor, instead of sending data to a cloud data center. Processing data where it is created gives faster responses, better privacy, lower bandwidth costs and offline operation. Edge AI runs on efficient chips like the NPUs in phones and AI PCs, NVIDIA Jetson modules and small GPUs, usually with compact, quantized models.

Edge AI vs cloud AI

Many products use both: a small on-device model handles quick, private tasks and hands harder requests to a large cloud model.

Where you already use edge AI

  • Smartphones: face unlock, photo enhancement, live transcription, on-device assistants and features like Apple Intelligence and Gemini Nano.
  • PCs: Copilot+ PCs with NPUs of at least 40 TOPS run features such as live captions and background effects. See What is an AI PC?.
  • Cars: driver assistance and self-driving systems must react instantly, so perception runs on board.
  • Smart cameras: detecting people, vehicles or packages without streaming all video to the cloud.
  • Factories: inspecting products on a production line in real time.
  • Robots and drones: navigation and object recognition with no network delay.
  • Healthcare devices: wearables that detect irregular heart rhythms on the device.
  • Retail: shelf monitoring and checkout systems.

The hardware behind edge AI

TOPS (trillions of operations per second) is the usual headline figure for edge chips; see TOPS vs TFLOPS. Real performance also depends on memory bandwidth and software support. NPUs are compared with GPUs and TPUs in NPU vs GPU vs TPU.

How models are made small enough for the edge

  • Quantization: storing weights in 8 or 4 bits instead of 16 or 32. See LLM quantization.
  • Distillation: training a small model to imitate a large one. See What is knowledge distillation?.
  • Pruning: removing unnecessary weights.
  • Efficient architectures: models designed for mobile, such as MobileNet and YOLO variants for vision and small language models for text.
  • Runtimes: tools like TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, Core ML, LiteRT (formerly TensorFlow Lite) and llama.cpp optimise models for specific chips.

Benefits of edge AI

1. Speed: decisions in milliseconds, essential for cars, robots and AR. 2. Privacy: sensitive data such as faces, voices and health readings can stay on the device. 3. Reliability: keeps working without an internet connection. 4. Lower bandwidth: only results, not raw video, need to be sent. 5. Cost: avoids paying for cloud compute on every request. 6. Energy: small models on efficient chips can use far less energy per task. See how much energy AI uses.

Challenges

  • Limited compute and memory: devices cannot run the largest models.
  • Power and heat: batteries and passive cooling limit sustained performance.
  • Fragmented hardware: each chip has its own tools and supported operations.
  • Updates and security: deploying and securing models on thousands of devices is complex.

Edge AI and local LLMs

Running a chatbot on your own laptop or desktop is also a form of edge AI. Small and mid-sized models now run well on consumer GPUs and Apple Silicon. See how to run an LLM locally, how much VRAM you need and the best GPU for local LLMs.

Frequently asked questions

Is edge AI the same as on-device AI?

Mostly yes. On-device AI is edge AI running on the end device itself. Edge AI can also include small servers placed close to where data is created, such as in a store or factory.

Do I need an NPU for edge AI?

No, but NPUs are the most power-efficient option on phones and laptops. GPUs and CPUs can also run edge models.

What is TinyML?

TinyML is machine learning on microcontrollers that use milliwatts of power, such as keyword detection ("Hey Siri") or vibration monitoring in machines.

Will edge AI replace cloud AI?

No. The biggest, most capable models will stay in the cloud. Edge and cloud AI complement each other.

Sources and further reading

  • NVIDIA, Jetson AGX Orin
  • Microsoft, Copilot+ PCs
  • Howard et al., MobileNets: Efficient Convolutional Neural Networks for Mobile Vision Applications (2017)
  • Google, LiteRT documentation

TITLE: What Is Knowledge Distillation? How Big AI Models Teach Small Ones
LABEL: EXPLAINER
EXCERPT: Knowledge distillation trains a small "student" model to imitate a large "teacher" model, keeping much of its ability at a fraction of the size and cost. How distillation works, soft labels, examples like DistilBERT and DeepSeek-R1 distilled models, benefits, limits and legal questions.
KEY: Knowledge distillation is a technique for compressing AI models: a large, capable teacher model generates outputs, and a smaller student model is trained to imitate them. The student ends up much faster and cheaper to run while keeping a large share of the teacher's ability. Distillation is behind many of today's efficient models, from DistilBERT, which kept about 97% of BERT's language understanding while being 40% smaller and 60% faster, to the small reasoning models DeepSeek distilled from R1.
content:
Short answer

Knowledge distillation is a technique for compressing AI models: a large, capable teacher model generates outputs, and a smaller student model is trained to imitate them. The student ends up much faster and cheaper to run while keeping a large share of the teacher's ability. Distillation is behind many of today's efficient models, from DistilBERT, which kept about 97% of BERT's language understanding while being 40% smaller and 60% faster, to the small reasoning models DeepSeek distilled from R1.

The idea in plain English

A student can learn a subject from a textbook (the raw data), but learns faster from an expert teacher who explains how they think, including which answers are almost right. Distillation gives a small model the teacher's richer guidance instead of only the "correct answers".

How distillation works

Classic distillation with soft labels

Geoffrey Hinton and colleagues formalised the method in 2015:

1. Train (or take) a large teacher model. 2. Run the teacher on training examples and record its full probability distribution over possible answers, called soft labels. For an image of a husky, the teacher might say 80% husky, 15% wolf, 5% malamute. 3. Train the student to match those probabilities, usually combined with the true labels.

Soft labels carry "dark knowledge": the teacher's sense of which wrong answers are close. A temperature setting softens the probabilities so these relationships are easier to learn, the same idea as the sampling temperature explained in LLM temperature, top-k and top-p.

Distillation for large language models

For large language models, common approaches are:

  • Logit distillation: the student matches the teacher's probability for every possible next token. Needs access to the teacher's internals.
  • Sequence-level distillation: the teacher writes complete answers, explanations or step-by-step reasoning, and the student is fine-tuned on that synthetic data. This works even when you only have API access to the teacher.
  • On-policy distillation: the student generates answers and the teacher scores or corrects them, so the student learns from its own mistakes.

Real examples

Many small language models owe much of their quality to distillation and synthetic training data generated by bigger models.

Why distillation matters

  • Lower cost: a smaller model needs fewer GPUs and less VRAM to serve, cutting inference costs dramatically.
  • Speed: fewer parameters means faster responses, because generation speed depends on how many bytes must be read from memory per token. See GPU memory bandwidth.
  • On-device AI: distilled models can run on phones, AI PCs and edge devices.
  • Energy: smaller models use less electricity per request. See how much energy AI uses.
  • Specialisation: a student can be distilled for one task, such as customer support or code completion, and match the teacher on that task.

Distillation vs quantization vs pruning

They are often combined: distil a smaller model, then quantize it to 4 bits to run locally.

Limitations

  • Capability ceiling: the student rarely exceeds the teacher and usually loses some breadth, especially on rare knowledge and complex reasoning.
  • Inherited flaws: biases and errors in the teacher pass to the student. See AI hallucinations.
  • Compute still needed: generating teacher outputs and training the student takes significant GPU time, though far less than training a large model from scratch. See AI training vs inference.

Legal and ethical questions

Most commercial AI providers' terms of service prohibit using their model outputs to train competing models. In early 2025, distillation became a public controversy when OpenAI said it was reviewing indications that its models' outputs had been used to train a rival model. Distilling from open-weight models is generally allowed, subject to each model's licence, so check the licence and terms before training on another model's outputs.

How to try distillation yourself

1. Pick a capable teacher (a large open model, or an API you are allowed to use for training). 2. Generate high-quality answers for a few thousand prompts in your domain. 3. Fine-tune a small model on those prompt-answer pairs, for example with QLoRA on a single GPU. 4. Evaluate the student against the teacher on held-out examples.

Our fine-tuning guide covers the tools and GPU memory you need.

Frequently asked questions

Is distillation the same as fine-tuning?

Distillation usually uses fine-tuning as its training method, but the defining feature is that the training targets come from a teacher model rather than human-written labels.

Can a distilled model be better than the teacher?

Occasionally on a narrow task, especially when combined with extra data or reinforcement learning, but generally the student is slightly weaker overall.

Why is it called distillation?

Like distilling a liquid to concentrate its essence, the process extracts the most useful knowledge from a big model into a smaller one.

Do distilled models run on consumer GPUs?

Yes, that is a main purpose. Distilled models of 1.5B to 14B parameters run well on 8 to 16 GB GPUs or Apple Silicon. See how to run an LLM locally.

Sources and further reading

  • Hinton, Vinyals and Dean, Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network (2015)
  • Sanh et al., DistilBERT, a distilled version of BERT (2019)
  • DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-R1 (2025)
  • Hugging Face, Knowledge distillation guide

TITLE: What Is Natural Language Processing (NLP)? How Computers Understand Language
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: Natural language processing (NLP) is the branch of AI that lets computers read, understand and generate human language. Core NLP tasks, how it evolved from rules to transformers and LLMs, everyday examples, and how to get started.
KEY: Natural language processing (NLP) is the field of artificial intelligence that enables computers to understand, interpret and generate human language, written or spoken. It powers search engines, translation, spam filters, voice assistants and chatbots. NLP has gone through three eras: hand-written rules, statistical machine learning, and today's deep learning with transformers, which produced large language models like GPT, Claude and Gemini that can handle almost any language task.
content:
Short answer

Natural language processing (NLP) is the field of artificial intelligence that enables computers to understand, interpret and generate human language, written or spoken. It powers search engines, translation, spam filters, voice assistants and chatbots. NLP has gone through three eras: hand-written rules, statistical machine learning, and today's deep learning with transformers, which produced large language models like GPT, Claude and Gemini that can handle almost any language task.

Why language is hard for computers

Human language is ambiguous and full of context. "I saw her duck" can mean two very different things. Words change meaning ("bank" of a river vs a bank account), sarcasm flips meaning, and the same idea can be expressed in endless ways. NLP is about turning this messy, flexible language into something a computer can work with, and back again.

Common NLP tasks

How NLP evolved

1. Rule-based NLP (1950s to 1980s)

Experts wrote grammar rules and dictionaries by hand. These systems worked in narrow domains but broke easily with real-world language.

2. Statistical NLP (1990s to 2010s)

Systems learned patterns from large text collections: counting which words appear together, then using models like n-grams, naive Bayes and conditional random fields. Statistical machine translation and early spam filters came from this era.

3. Neural NLP and word embeddings (2013 onwards)

Word2vec (2013) represented words as vectors so that similar words sit close together, see What are embeddings?. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs and LSTMs) then processed sentences word by word.

4. Transformers and LLMs (2017 onwards)

The transformer architecture (2017) used attention to look at all words at once, which trained faster and captured long-range meaning. BERT (2018) set new records on understanding tasks, and the GPT series showed that one model trained to predict the next word could do translation, summarisation, question answering and more. Today most NLP tasks are handled by a single large language model with a good prompt, or by a smaller model fine-tuned for one task.

How modern NLP works, step by step

1. Tokenization: text is split into tokens, words or word pieces. 2. Embedding: each token becomes a vector of numbers. 3. Contextual processing: transformer layers update each token's vector based on the surrounding words, so "bank" gets a different representation in different sentences. 4. Task output: the model produces a label, extracts spans of text or generates new text one token at a time.

NLP in everyday life

  • Search engines understanding what you mean, not just matching keywords
  • Autocomplete and grammar correction in keyboards and email
  • Voice assistants and dictation
  • Translation in browsers and apps
  • Customer service chatbots and email routing
  • Social media moderation and spam filtering
  • Medical and legal document analysis
  • Coding assistants that turn instructions into code

NLP vs LLMs vs NLU

  • NLP is the whole field.
  • NLU (natural language understanding) focuses on comprehension: intent, meaning, entities.
  • NLG (natural language generation) focuses on producing text.
  • LLMs are a powerful technology within NLP that now handles both understanding and generation.

Challenges that remain

  • Hallucinations: generative models can state false information confidently. See AI hallucinations.
  • Bias: models can reflect stereotypes in training data.
  • Low-resource languages: many of the world's languages have little digital text, so models perform worse in them, and they often need more tokens per word.
  • Cost: large models need expensive GPUs to train and serve. See AI training vs inference.

How to get started with NLP

  • No code: use an LLM chat app to classify, summarise or extract information with clear prompts.
  • Python: libraries such as Hugging Face Transformers, spaCy and NLTK cover most tasks.
  • Local models: run open models on your own computer for private text processing; see how to run an LLM locally.

Frequently asked questions

Is ChatGPT an example of NLP?

Yes. ChatGPT is built on large language models, the most advanced form of NLP today.

What is the difference between NLP and machine learning?

Machine learning is a general method for learning from data. NLP is an application area focused on language, which today relies mostly on machine learning and deep learning.

Is NLP still a good career?

Yes, though the work has shifted from building task-specific models towards building applications with LLMs, retrieval, evaluation and fine-tuning.

Does NLP include speech?

Speech recognition and text-to-speech are closely related fields often grouped with NLP. Modern multimodal models handle speech and text together.

Sources and further reading

  • Jurafsky and Martin, Speech and Language Processing (3rd edition draft)
  • Mikolov et al., Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space (2013)
  • Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (2017)
  • Devlin et al., BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding (2018)

TITLE: What Is Reinforcement Learning? How AI Learns by Trial and Error (With Examples)
LABEL: GUIDE
EXCERPT: Reinforcement learning (RL) teaches an AI agent to make decisions by rewarding good actions and penalising bad ones. How RL works, key terms like policy and reward, famous examples from AlphaGo to ChatGPT and reasoning models, and its limits.
KEY: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a type of machine learning in which an agent learns by trial and error: it takes actions in an environment, receives rewards or penalties, and gradually learns a strategy (a policy) that earns the most reward over time. RL powered DeepMind's AlphaGo, helps robots learn to walk, and is a key ingredient in modern AI assistants: RLHF made ChatGPT helpful, and large-scale RL is what turns language models into reasoning models.
content:
Short answer

Reinforcement learning (RL) is a type of machine learning in which an agent learns by trial and error: it takes actions in an environment, receives rewards or penalties, and gradually learns a strategy (a policy) that earns the most reward over time. RL powered DeepMind's AlphaGo, helps robots learn to walk, and is a key ingredient in modern AI assistants: RLHF made ChatGPT helpful, and large-scale RL is what turns language models into reasoning models.

RL in plain English

Think of training a dog. You do not explain the rules; you reward the behaviour you want. Over many attempts, the dog learns which actions lead to treats. Reinforcement learning works the same way, except the "dog" is a computer program and the "treat" is a number.

How reinforcement learning compares with other machine learning

For how these fit into AI as a whole, see AI vs machine learning vs deep learning.

Key terms

  • Agent: the learner and decision maker.
  • Environment: the world the agent acts in, such as a game, a simulator or a conversation.
  • State: what the agent observes at a given moment.
  • Action: a choice the agent makes.
  • Reward: a number that says how good the outcome was.
  • Policy: the agent's strategy, mapping states to actions.
  • Value: the expected future reward from a state or action.
  • Episode: one complete run, such as one game.

How the learning loop works

1. The agent observes the current state. 2. It chooses an action using its policy. 3. The environment changes and returns a reward. 4. The agent updates its policy to make rewarding actions more likely. 5. Repeat millions of times.

A central challenge is exploration vs exploitation: should the agent try something new that might be better, or stick with what already works? Another is credit assignment: when a game is won after 200 moves, which moves deserve the credit?

Main approaches

  • Value-based methods such as Q-learning learn how good each action is in each state, then pick the best. DeepMind's DQN used a neural network to play dozens of Atari games from raw pixels in 2013 to 2015.
  • Policy-based methods directly adjust the policy to increase reward. PPO (proximal policy optimization) is one of the most widely used.
  • Actor-critic methods combine both: an "actor" chooses actions and a "critic" estimates their value.
  • Model-based methods learn a model of the environment and plan ahead, as in AlphaZero and MuZero.

Combining RL with deep neural networks is called deep reinforcement learning.

Famous examples

  • AlphaGo (2016): beat world champion Lee Sedol 4–1 at Go, a game long thought too complex for computers. Its successor AlphaZero learned chess, shogi and Go from self-play alone.
  • Games: OpenAI Five (Dota 2) and DeepMind's AlphaStar (StarCraft II) reached top human levels.
  • Robotics: robots learn to walk, grasp and manipulate objects, often in simulation first.
  • Chip design and data centers: RL has been used to optimise chip layouts and cooling systems.
  • Recommendation and ads: systems that optimise long-term engagement.

RL in ChatGPT and modern LLMs

RLHF: making models helpful

After pre-training, a large language model is good at predicting text but not at being a helpful assistant. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) fixes this: people rank model answers, a reward model learns those preferences, and the LLM is trained with RL to produce answers the reward model scores highly. This was central to ChatGPT; see How does ChatGPT work?.

RL for reasoning

Since 2024, labs have applied RL on problems with checkable answers, such as maths and code with tests. Models are rewarded for correct final answers and learn to think step by step, check their work and backtrack. OpenAI's o1 and DeepSeek-R1 (which used an efficient method called GRPO) showed how powerful this is.

Agents

RL is increasingly used to train AI agents that use tools, browse and write code over many steps, rewarding them for completing real tasks.

Limitations

  • Reward hacking: agents find loopholes that earn reward without doing what designers wanted, a key concern in AI alignment.
  • Sample inefficiency: RL often needs millions of attempts, which is why simulators matter.
  • Instability: training can be sensitive to settings and hard to reproduce.
  • Sim-to-real gap: skills learned in simulation may not transfer perfectly to the physical world.
  • Reward design: defining the right reward for real-world goals is hard.

What hardware RL needs

RL training alternates between generating experience (running the policy many times) and updating the model. For LLMs, the generation phase is essentially large-scale inference, so RL for reasoning models uses huge GPU clusters for both sampling and training. Small RL projects (games, simple robots) run fine on a single consumer GPU.

Frequently asked questions

Is reinforcement learning the same as deep learning?

No. Deep learning is about using deep neural networks; RL is about learning from rewards. Deep reinforcement learning combines the two.

Who invented reinforcement learning?

Its modern foundations were developed by Richard Sutton and Andrew Barto in the 1980s, building on earlier ideas from psychology and control theory. They received the 2024 ACM Turing Award for this work.

Is RLHF still used?

Yes, along with related methods such as DPO and RL from AI feedback. Most assistant models use some form of preference training after supervised fine-tuning.

Can I learn RL as a beginner?

Yes. Start with simple environments in the open-source Gymnasium library and classic algorithms like Q-learning, then move to deep RL libraries.

Sources and further reading

  • Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd edition)
  • Mnih et al., Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning (Nature, 2015)
  • Silver et al., Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search (Nature, 2016)
  • Ouyang et al., Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (2022)
  • DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-R1 (2025)
